idiom_name: per-dependency capacity partition (permits or dedicated workers) + explicit saturation policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: for each dependency (or tenant, or priority class) define a dedicated capacity partition - either a fixed number of permits acquired before each call and released after it, or a dedicated set of workers with a bounded queue. Choose the isolation mechanism from the failure domain: permits bound concurrent calls while leaving threads shared; dedicated workers keep a blocking dependency from occupying shared threads; separate pools, processes or containers provide harder isolation when the underlying resource is shared. Make saturation explicit - fail fast with a distinguishable error, or wait with a bounded timeout behind a bounded queue, never unbounded queueing. Size every limit from measured concurrency (expected concurrent calls plus headroom), keep the sum of all partitions inside the host's capacity, and instrument admission, saturation and queue depth per partition. The classic pool/thread structure remains justified when calls block threads; for suspending or asynchronous calls a permit counter is usually the whole pattern.
code_sketch:
db   = partition(permits=8, queue=16, on_full=reject)   # one partition per dependency
db.acquire_or_reject()
try:
    row = call(db_dependency, request)
finally:
    db.release()                    # every exit path frees the slot
# worker-isolation partition instead:
db_workers = pool(size=8, queue=16, on_full=reject)
db_workers.submit(request)
pitfalls: Using one global limiter as a bulkhead -> a hot dependency still consumes every permit -> create one partition per dependency, tenant, or priority class.
Bounding concurrency while leaving the wait queue unbounded -> overload becomes unbounded latency and memory growth -> cap the queue and reject or cancel excess work.
Running blocking work inside a non-blocking partition -> caller or event-loop threads starve while permits remain occupied -> use a dedicated executor or worker bulkhead for blocking calls.
Sizing partitions independently of the host budget -> the sum oversubscribes CPU, threads, connections, or file descriptors -> budget the partitions together and reserve headroom.
Releasing permits only on the success path -> an exception leaks capacity until the partition stays saturated -> release in finally, defer, RAII, or an equivalent scope guard.

Setting semaphore maxWaitDuration too high for interactive paths -> callers park behind saturation and the latency bound disappears -> use immediate or short bounded admission and map rejection explicitly.

Returning raw bulkhead-full errors without a fallback policy -> callers receive an opaque failure even when stale or deferred work is acceptable -> map rejection to a typed response, cache, or deferred queue.
Keeping a saturated pool without a circuit breaker -> futile calls continue occupying every slot while the downstream is sick -> combine capacity isolation with timeout and circuit breaking.

Putting per-dependency limits below one shared connection or executor pool -> the shared pool still exhausts and unrelated calls queue together -> partition the resource owner or enforce the hard bound above it.
Choosing a partition key for convenience rather than failure domain -> tenants or priorities that share a cell still become noisy neighbors -> choose a stable key and verify blast radius under load.

Measuring rejection alone -> long calls and queue waits can consume capacity without producing rejections -> instrument active work, queue depth, wait time, timeouts, completions, and rejections per partition.

Deep queuing on a synchronous bulkhead -> queued delegates hold threads while waiting for a slot, so thread exhaustion returns with extra steps -> keep the sync queue at 0-1 entries and queue only async I/O paths.

Over-partitioning out of resilience anxiety -> dozens of tiny pools strand idle capacity and become mis-tuned configuration nobody revisits -> start coarse at the real failure domain and split further only when telemetry shows a noisy neighbor.

Treating a hand-tuned static limit as permanent -> latency shifts and traffic-mix changes silently turn it into premature rejection or admitted overload -> re-derive limits from telemetry or adopt adaptive concurrency limiting such as Netflix concurrency-limits.
sources: Nygard, M. - Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2018)
